248.t: Fiddle players: Peter Bocage, Manuel Manetta, Freddie Keppard
248.s: Dawson names Peter Bocage and others as good violinists, says Freddie Keppard started on violin, and that these men all read music at sight.
248.ch: String bands, serenading and violin players
248.q: No, he had a heavy band. Mm-hmm. But he was a good violin player. Mario Mineta was a good violin player. Uh, uh, uh, let's see, Freddie Kepard. Freddie, Freddie Kepard started on a violin when he started playing, before he took up trumpet. Mm-hmm. Uh, I see.

248.t: Solo players, violinists and the Lindsey family
248.s: Dawson says there were no solo players, repeats that Palao, Manetta and Bocage were fine sight-readers, and recalls the Lindsey bass player.
248.ch: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
248.q: I didn't have a band on them, so. Jimm Apollo was a good violin player, though. He was just like, he was classed just like Emmanuel, uh, Man Manera and, uh, uh, uh, Peter Bocot. All of them good violin players. Sight readers.

248.s: Dawson ranks Palao first, Manetta, Bocage, Valto and Tinette next.
248.q: I think, to my, to my idea, I think, uh, uh, I believe, uh, uh, uh, Jim Apala, I think Jim Apala was about the best violin, violin player. And, uh, well, Peter Bocos, he, he was good. I think, now let's see, uh, uh, after, after Jim Apala, I think Peter Bocos came second. Now, Manu Mineta used to…

248.t: Rene Batiste and the violinist Ferdinand Valteau
248.s: Dawson barely knew Rene Batiste and remembers old man Valteau as a good violinist who freelanced and never held a regular band job.
248.ch: Learning, lawn parties and band rivalries
248.q: Yeah, Batiste, yeah. I believe I heard of him, huh? I didn't know him much. You didn't know that? No, I didn't know much about him.

763.t: Hot fiddlers and his own string trios
763.s: Discusses violinists Oscar Marco, Dave Perkins, Batiste O'Quinn, and his own violin-guitar-bass groups on Decatur Street.
763.q: Yeah. Mama Langan used to talk about him. Batiste O'Quinn. It goes to show you what I'm telling you. It's not no line because they can verify it, you know? But then it's all the men I played. And without counting the men that I've learned myself, you know? Learned them how to play bass. Learned…

763.t: Violins in dance bands; Max Fink
763.s: Dance bands rarely used violins; first with a violin was Pete Herman's Black Orchard with the Marco brothers; Max Fink was a straight violinist.
763.q: No, no dance bands. No violins at all. They didn't do it? All the dance bands that they had was just reed, brass, and string. I mean, it falls to bass, what do you call it? Yeah. But I mean, they didn't have the... But there was no such thing as violins or nothing. The first band that I played were…

38.t: Willie Jones and early jazz fiddle in New Orleans
38.s: A boyhood friend, Willie Jones, played jazz fiddle and showed the others the extra notes. Jimmy Palao is mentioned.
38.q: Yes, we had one boy that, he was better than all of us. He had a darn good ear, and he played a few of those ragged notes on the fiddle, and he showed us how to do them, and he said he was playing this big melody, and all the tunes that were out then.

38.t: Jimmy Bell, violinist at the Grand Theater
38.s: Levy recalls Jimmy Bell as a strong violinist at the Grand Theater and says he arranged for Bell's band.
38.q: Jimmy Bell played a very good violin, very strong too. He played the Grand Theater, you know, in the pit there. And then he had a band of his own. I made some arrangements for Jimmy Bell's band too.

293.t: Violinists: Peter Williams, Piron and Sam Morgan's band
293.s: Third reel begins with Sam Morgan, then violinists, including Piron, a reading jazz violinist who led a six-piece band at the lake.
293.ch: Violinists, Jimmy Noon and Decatur Street
293.q: You heard him, man? Yeah. P-Rone was a good violinist. He was a jazz violinist, you know what I mean? Uh-huh. And he read music. He was first class. He used to play, he played out there on the lake for I don't know how long. Oh, I bought tranchinas? Tranchinas, that's right. That's why he played…

293.t: Violin-led string bands in the district
293.s: Violin led the four or five piece bands in the district, such as Piron, Paul Dominguez and Valto.
293.q: Well, Paul Dominguez played and I can't call this man's name. He played. Oh, I can't, he was a violin player. In them days lots of guys was playing violin. Can't call that gentleman's name to say my life. Piron was one. Piron played in the district many times and this fellow played and…

650.t: Violinists: Herbert Lindsay and his double stops
650.s: Amacker names the greatest violinist in the city, Herbert Lindsay, called Fiddle Up, famed for his double stops.
650.q: Man he was a wizard He was a wizard Fiddle Up He was a wizard He could One thing he could do With a violin That as much as Any man on earth Could do And it was very Important to do That on violin He could make As many double stops Any man ever lived Really? He could make As many double stops As any…

650.t: Violinist Herbert Lindsay and his double stops
650.s: Lindsay was a crackerjack violinist who played double stops, and worked in all the downtown bands including Piron's and Pete Lala's.
650.q: Now, Herbert Lindsay, that was a crackerjack violin player. He was one of the best. Now, you call the man's name there. He was one of the best violinists that I would listen to for this particular reason. Herbert Lindsay could make more, yet, listen, yet he's an air player. But he could make more…

15.t: His violin technique, a promise to record on fiddle and fiddle with Oliver
15.s: Howard says he plays violin better than clarinet, promises to record on fiddle sometime, and says he played it with Oliver only in shows.
15.ch: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
15.q: Because it's, yeah. I do. You're crazy if you don't play it. I want to make some records with you on violin. Hey, I'm getting paid to play clarinet here. Truthfully. You're what? I'm being paid to play clarinet here. I ain't going to bring no fiddle in there. No, but I'll make some records with…

15.t: Violinists Paul Dominguez and Armand Piron compared
15.s: Howard knew Dominguez and Piron and says their violin playing was more embellished variations than his own.
15.ch: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
15.q: Oh well I think he played more saxophone than he did violin. He played, I think it was ten saxophone. I mean the way he played violin.

824.s: Gallodoro tells how Jascha Heifetz told Venuti he could have been a great concert violinist, citing his intonation on the album.

824.t: Willcox on Joe Venuti and Stephane Grappelli
824.s: Willcox praises Venuti as capable of any symphony and compares his playing to Grappelli's; they joke about Grappelli's nationality.
824.q: You know Joe Venuti, now there’s a guy that I’ll bet any amount of money that he could step in any symphony, but there’s many a symphony guy that can play like Joe maybe in

173.t: John Gould, a violinist who played by ear
173.s: He admired Gould, a Black violinist who played with guitar and bass trio and never read music, whom he heard when he was about 19-20.
173.q: Oh, I must have been about 19, 20 years of age. About that time? Yeah. That was shortly before, I think that I got started with music.

689.t: New Orleans violinists: Peter Bocage and the Bigards
689.s: Peter Bocage is praised as a violinist; Emile Bigard is discussed as Barney Bigard's uncle and a heavier player.
689.q: But when you talk about I want to pick around for violin, opera, jazz, anything you want to play. Anything you put before those guys. They played Peter Bocard's nice violin play too. Peter Bocard's very good violinist.

179.t: Violinists, Robichaux, Kimball and Percy Humphrey's band
179.s: Professor violinists read strictly; John Robichaux's music; Kimball now with Percy Humphrey; Willie Humphrey; Oil Humphrey's drinking.
179.q: Lord George Lewis is about the best I know about head well the violin players I know was up with Pierrot and Peter yeah and Manuel them and all the three violin players I know during that time

457.t: Violin in New Orleans dance bands
457.s: Violins played lead in dance orchestras, with clarinet central in Dixieland groups; some improvised.
457.q: No. No. No. Not as much as the clarinet because... Having... More or less on the Dixon Land idea, there was always that clarinet.

949.t: Bob Matthews, vibes, and the planned trio
949.s: Drummer and vibist Bob Matthews bridged modern and traditional jazz for him, disliked New Orleans jazz, and planned a guitar-vibes-violin trio with Bill Russell.
949.q: Uh, who's, uh, I don't know who is Bob Matthews? Yeah. He was a drummer. He's from a, Decatur, George. I can tell you about him. Very interesting, very interesting guy. Very intense.

259.t: Mandolin and violin players, and the Humphreys
259.s: He names mandolin and violin players including Jim Humphrey, Johnny Delpy, Peter Bocage and Mario Minelli.
259.q: How about some of the good mandolin players used to be here? Who? Mandolin players. Mandolin. Mandolin. Mandolin players? Yeah. Mandolin players. They need girls. They could play. They could play minor. And the man Humphrey, he had a bad. The old man, that's good. He had a bad.

474.t: Joe Gabriel playing at his grocery
474.s: Playing violin and rhythm with Joe Gabriel at his grocery.
474.ch: New Orleans bands: Cheek, Parker, Morgan
474.q: In his house, back in the house. Yeah. Oh yeah in the grocery store and played with him. See he used to get his violin and me and him used to sit down and drink wine together and you know, serenade on things like 12th Street Rag you know, or some old number that you know, in the background like…

33.t: Second reel: why violins faded from dance bands and carnival balls
33.s: DeDroit says violins did not fit two-beat music and he kept only one for carnival balls and shows.
33.ch: Strings, arrangements and the Shrine band
33.q: Well I think the thing, the violins didn't fit with two beat music. They could play it, but I mean it didn't fit in that combination and he'd sit there most of the time if he didn't pluck it he'd have it as a rap. You know what I mean? I used the violin to play the shows and I'd let him go. I…

773.t: Sidney Vinn, Matoya and the violinist Pierron
773.s: Pictures she did not have; violinist Pierron with one short leg who played at West End.
773.q: He had a little foot, you know, and it kind of, was short and wet up, you know. But a fine little fella, fine musician.

14.t: Paul Weyer, the Pensacola violinist and pool shark
14.s: Love describes Paul Weyer from Pensacola as a gifted violinist and gambler who played Cavalleria for the band and stole the pool ball.
14.q: Yeah. Him and his brother, they had a band there. Well I guess all them fellas played together. He was a good violin player. He used to come around where our band was, you know, we had a little joint where we used to sit around there until it was time to go to work. We was working over the bar…

2.t: Jelly's term 'legitimate' and violin players in New Orleans bands
2.s: The article 'Jazz in the 20s', Jelly's remarks on legitimate violinists and why bands hired a reader like Manuel Manetta.
2.q: Yeah, a lot of other people. In fact, Jelly used that term too. I was talking about violin players, which Jelly didn't use hardly ever, as far as I know he did use on one of his records, Someday Sweetheart. But he evidently didn't look with too much favor on violins. He said even in New Orleans,…

601.t: The violinist Valto and the Onward band
601.s: Russell asks about a violin player called Valto, who lived on this side of the river. Neither man knows more. Martin mentions Jimmy Polar and Manuel coming up with the Onward band.
601.q: Valto, that's all I know is Valto. You take, uh, the violin player back up in there, who that was? Uh, no. Jimmy Polar in there, man. Over the river there. But he was living over the river. Yeah.

279.s: Oscar Marco's violin style is compared to Joe Venuti.
279.q: Yes, he was a fine violinist. Oscar Marco played really, really great violin. I can remember him playing fine violin. His brother Mickey Marco was a very good pianist too.

800.t: Playing with violinists: Robichaux and others
800.s: He did not care for violin because violinists were bosses; he rates Dominguez and Bocage and calls Robichaux a businessman.
800.q: I didn't care about violin. Well? I don't like playing. I didn't care too much about violin. But they were the boss all the time. A lot of the violin players used to be leaders. They were leaders. They used to run the outfit. They run the outfit. Like Eugene Deeson. No, not Eugene Deeson. Paul…

191.t: Reel two begins: Max Fink and New Orleans violinists
191.s: Allen resumes on the second reel and asks about Max Fink; Kelly describes him as a violinist in New Orleans theaters and carnival balls, and mentions Ted Frank.
191.q: before your time. He was a violinist and a very extremely popular character in New Orleans history. Played in the theaters and played for all the carnival balls and things like that. Well, Ted Frank, yes. I loved Ted Frank and I knew his father before him. And Dave who established the sheet meat…

776.s: Only Piron had a violin; before amplification Charlie Herzog's violin could not be heard.
776.q: And in the early days when they had this orchestra on the J.S. From the little Charlie Herzog. He played the violin in the early days. Otherwise, not much on the violin. You couldn't hear it for one thing. And if you played the band, they were soft enough that you could hear the violin. And they…

819.t: Yellow Nunez and violinist Max Fink
819.s: Clarinetist Yellow Nunez and violin players, with Max Fink as the reading man of the day.
819.q: No, no. Yellow, as far as I know, didn't play in a cab right where I was. Oh, yeah. I doubt if he could play for the singers in those days.

283.s: He describes Venuti as a crazy but wonderful fiddler on radio and mentions friend Jerry Colonna sitting in at the Famous Door.
283.q: Yeah. Uh, Joe's a crazy guy, buddy. He's a wonderful fiddle player, man. Oh, yeah. And he's good. You put him on a radio with you, man, he make you laugh. You... Yeah. I went, uh, with him, uh, on a radio program one night. I couldn't stop laughing. The guy's so crazy. But you see, Joe Venuti…

288.t: Reel change; Crescent Band, Superior band and Peter Bocage
288.s: Back on tape, Charles contrasts Ory and the Crescent band (no music) with the Superior band's violinist Peter Bocage.
288.ch: Society work, Camilla Todd and Storyville
288.q: I said the Crescent Band and Ori during those days, that was, you know, that was really getting work. Of course they had a lot of little bands that was playing but they didn't play no music at all. But Ori and the Crescent, Jack Kerrin there, was the only band that didn't use no music at all. You…

572.t: Violinists: Harry Hoffman, Joe Venuti and Eddie South
572.s: They discuss jazz fiddlers, with praise for Harry Hoffman and Venuti's priority.
572.ch: Wider talk: bands, places and players
572.q: And the name was, uh, I can't think of his name now. He played a lot, a lot of things. He, he played with, uh, with, uh, with the bow and then strings over, like, like Joe Benuti did. Mm-hmm. He played a lot of stuff like, yeah, well, it's just, uh, Harry, Harry Hoffman or something like that.

880.t: Violin talk and where the Ory photograph came from
880.s: Joseph on playing violin; the men study the photo's setting and Joseph says he got it from John Porter about five years earlier.
880.q: It would take me long to play something. In fact, I could play something in about half an hour. I could play almost enough to play a little dance. I could play a little violin too. You know what kind of violin play out? Years ago, people hardly knew anything about violin.

290.s: Violin was used only when a clarinet or sax was unavailable; bands relied on trumpet and clarinet.
290.ch: Sam Morgan, repertoire and Silver Leaf
290.q: Well, they used to use violin, sometimes they would need an extra man and they couldn't get a clarinet or a saxophone, then they would use violin. A lot of bands didn't like to use a violin. For what reason? Oh, they found it was too light, too soft. It didn't produce what they wanted.

484.t: Frankie Dusen, Algiers violinists, Robichaux and Bocage
484.s: Brownlee does not know Dusen, then recalls violinists Robichaux, Charlie Devergis, Al Minetta and Pete Bocage, and the Charlie Love records.
484.q: I'm sure you heard him. Well, it might be just, I, I, no doubt I heard him, just like I was talking about Kid Thomas and I was talking about somebody else. Uh. Peter Volcage. Well, Peter Volcage, yeah, well, he was, he was all right. And then there used to be a violinist, too, that was quite a, one…

909.t: Batiste, John Robichaux and the Silver Leaf band
909.s: The Silver Leaf band, the violinists Batiste and Robichaux as partners and teachers, strict reading and rehearsals, and Robichaux's sidemen.
909.q: Yeah I got a straight See, him and John Robichaud was partners Them was two violinists And one would get a rich job Well, Robichaud couldn't get off him But Batiste, we was out in the field, you see And everything Robichaud would get Well, just like If I'm connected with another band If I get…

766.t: The violinist Dominguez compared to others
766.s: Dominguez was a jazz violinist, not in the class of the older violinists, and played with Milton's band.
766.q: He wasn't in their class, no. He was like a jazz violin player, something like Willie. That's all I was with Saeed, Willie Durner was. Playin' the thing he helped. He could read too, but I mean that'd be most of you and I could play that. The jazz violin. And Paul Delingrich. Yeah. That's when old…

58.t: Reading bands and violin players in New Orleans
58.s: Punch names reading bands such as the Tuxedo and the Josephs, and violinists.
58.ch: Trumpet styles and early New Orleans scene
58.q: I can't call his name, I couldn't call it for you. He's down there on, on, on, first of the living room, I got a barbershop. Oh yeah.

128.t: Violinists and Big Eye Louis Nelson's reading
128.s: Robinson lists violin players including Bocage, and discusses Big Eye Lewis and the importance of reading and executing.
128.q: take the time, see Big, he meets every fellow there, you see, he gets with a bunch of musicians like that, and he can play something there, the music, you understand? You can disqualify that, know what I mean? Mmhmm. You can disqualify them, you understand? Then you meet the fellow there, what can…

371.s: Jones recalls writing out solos for violinist Louis Eeley and learning of his death.
371.q: Oh, that violin player. I had done some dates with this violinist, some recording dates. He seemed to be very fluent. He was a good player. Most of violinists are not great jazz players whether you are talking about Shep Smith, or… Who is the other great jazz violinist? There are not too many.

226.t: Stuff Smith as a jazz violinist
226.s: He calls Stuff Smith the greatest jazz violinist, playing like a trumpeter and self-taught, unlike gypsy-style players.
226.q: Stuff, he had a reputation as one of the greatest jazz violinists. In my estimation, I haven’t heard anybody to compare with him yet, not as a jazz violinist.

104.t: Joe Venuti, a wild but great player
104.s: She describes Venuti as a vibrant, outrageous character and wonderful violinist whom she met at The Composer and recorded with.
104.q: I’d hear of Joe Venuti. He’s somebody I knew from the start. I’d heard of him in different bands. I think I met him at this very room, The Composer room. He was a guy that was . . . like a very lively, vibrant guy who’d say anything . . . lot of terrible stories about him, because he was just wild.…

400.t: Violin players survive by rolling cigars; the bass violin takes over
400.s: Out-of-work violinists rolled cigars; small clubs preferred bass violin to the noisy bass horn.
400.ch: Chicago childhood: theaters, violin and first bass
400.q: and all these guys are dressed very nice, the majority of them are dressed very nice, and they come down to the union hall in good shape. They didn‟t look like they were quite financially… and I wondered what happened, how did they do this? I found out, they were cigar makers.

566.t: Stuff Smith's band at the Hotel Vendome in Buffalo
566.s: Luke Stewart, Jonah Jones and Tom played at the Hotel Vendome in Buffalo in a band with Stuff Smith, whose violin and singing she admired. She also praises violinist Ginger Smock.
566.q: Yeah. But I always enjoyed his violin. You know you didn't hear people play violin like that.

99.s: Violinist Stuff Smith joined in Lexington in 1927, was put out front by Trent, and roomed and played all day with Pillars.
99.q: Stuff Smith. He was born in Portsmouth, Ohio. Stuff and I -- he joined Trent's Treb's band in Lexington, Kentucky in 1927, the fall of 1927. Stuff Smith joined our band then. And after he played, you know, on the bandstand with us, Alphonso Trent Treb took Stuff and put him out front, and then…

96.t: Playing a society party for Jascha Heifetz
96.s: At a Palm Beach society party, Heifetz asks 'what, no violins?' and remarks that at least you can dance to jazz.
96.q: No, he wasn't starving. I should tell you a little incident that happened down there. We played, we did play a job. They got one job for us, a one nighter at the Everglades. Vic Moore got it for us in Palm Beach and we were playing at this party, it was, you know, a society party. And we're playing…

428.t: Violinists Hall played with, from Stuff Smith to Wesley Robinson
428.s: Hall lists the jazz violinists he played with and a Philadelphia fiddler who rivalled Stuff Smith.
428.ch: Violinists, Stuff Smith and Josh White
428.q: Are we on now? Well, when you mention -- when -- Stuff Smith gave me an idea of all the violins that (inaudible) played with, starting from Woodie Guthrie on the one string fiddle for Asch Records, and I played with all the violinists that -- all the noted violinists through Eddie South and Joe…

529.t: Thad Jones and violinist Ray Perry sit in
529.s: Thad Jones loses his job by sitting in nightly, and Sam praises Ray Perry's Parker-like jazz violin and the Perry brothers.
529.q: Thad Jones used to come down there then. Well, Thad Jones got fired from messing around--down there messing around with us. He wouldn't go to work. He came down there playing with us every night. And, you know, when he decided to go to work, he didn't have no job.

13.t: Darnell Howard's fiddle and Joe Venuti sitting in
13.s: Venuti sat in at the Terrace.
13.ch: Swing, singers, Ed Fox and recordings
13.q: I'm trying to think, were they in the band at the same time I don't think they were in the band at the same time.
